newsitem.title: UK: Copper hits six month high as stocks dwindle.
newsitem.headline: Copper hits six month high as stocks dwindle.

text.p: Copper prices rose above $2,300 a tonne on Thursday, the highest since the Sumitomo Corp scandal erupted in June, as critically low inventory levels forced buyers to scramble for metal, traders and analysts said.
Copper traded up to $2,313 a tonne, compared to $2,272 on Wednesday, with traders noting that stocks of copper in U.S. market warehouses dropped by 1,268 short tons.
"It (the advance) is about options, and the concerns over the stocks," analyst Martin Squires of London Metal Exchange (LME) trader Rudolf Wolff and Co said.
On the LME, inventory levels dwindled rapidly to 6-1/4 year lows of just 90,050 tonnes, against 275,775 tonnes in September.

Significant tonnages of copper have been shipped out of the LME's European warehouses to satisfy voracious demand from the Far East, although traders are puzzled about how much is intended for actual use.
"A lot of it has gone to China, but we expect that some of it will start to re-materialise soon," said Squires.
Copper's strength has surprised many who counted out the metal in the wake of shockwaves from the Sumitomo affair.
In June, the Japanese conglomerate fired its head copper trader Yasuo Hamanaka, alleging he admitted running up losses of $2.6 billion in unauthorised copper trading.

As Hamanaka's dealing allegedly held copper prices artificially high for years, investors looking for good returns poured money into new mines around the world and a wave of new supplies is expected to hit the market in 1997 and 1998.
But the impact of this has been negated by a shortage of scrap since June, as scrap refiners' margins became prohibitive when copper prices fell to a low of $1,745 a tonne.
Because there was little scrap, fabricators turned towards refined copper, snapping up the limited supplies, analysts said.
The genuine shortage of metal and scrap has caused LME cash metal prices to soar above forward delivery values, a situation known as backwardation.
On Thursday, the cash premium over three months was at $280 a tonne, against the small discount or contango (the opposite of backwardation) that prevailed in September.
Another factor behind copper's remorseless rise has been the influence of options. These give the holder the right but not the obligation to buy or sell metal at set prices in the future.
The price advances of the last few weeks mean that many upside option positions that seemed destined to be abandoned are now likely to be exercised.

Traders who granted call options (meaning they would have to sell to the option holder on demand) are having to cover their commitments by buying metal as it becomes increasingly likely that the contracts will be exercised.
"I would not like to try and predict where this market is going," one trader said. "It could drop $50 in the bat of an eyelid. But equally it could go chasing up to $2,400 in the next few days."
